Cieled
sēld
v. part. (paneled, wainscoted; rendering Hebrew saphan and chaphah)
The old spelling of ceiled, from a root meaning to cover or overlay — whence our word ceiling. In Scripture the covering is usually costly cedar or fir paneling.

Biblical Definition

To be cieled is to be lined with fine paneling. Haggai turns the word into an indictment: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The greater house of the temple was cieled with fir and gold (2Ch 3:5); the scandal of Haggai's generation was private luxury financed by sanctuary neglect. Jeremiah adds the matching woe on the king who builds wide chambers “cieled with cedar” by unrighteousness (Jer 22:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ciel as to overlay or cover the inner roof of a building, and cieled as overlaid with a ceiling — citing 2 Chronicles 3.

CIELED, pp. Overlaid with a ceiling. 2 Chron. 3.

CIEL, v.t. To overlay or cover the inner roof of a building; to make a ceiling.

Key Scripture

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

2Ch 3:5 — "And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains."

Jer 22:14 — "That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion."

Hag 1:7 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways."

Modern Corruption

Modern versions read paneled houses, and the sting survives translation; what the church corrupts is the audit itself, having learned to call sanctuary-starving comfort by the name of stewardship.

expand to see more

Haggai's question is a comparison of ceilings. The people's houses were finished to the last panel while the LORD's house lay in rubble, and the prophet's remedy is not guilt but attention: “Consider your ways” (Hag 1:7). The cieled house is not condemned for its cedar — the temple itself was cieled — but for the waste next door that funded it.

Jeremiah's woe lands on Jehoiakim, who cieled his chambers with cedar while paying no wages (Jer 22:13–14), and the verdict redefines royalty: “he judged the cause of the poor and needy… was not this to know me? saith the LORD” (Jer 22:16). Paneling is honest wealth or plundered wages depending on what it cost the neighbour — and God reads the invoice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew saphan (H5603), to cover or panel, gives Haggai and Jeremiah their cieled houses; chaphah (H2645), to overlay, ciels the temple with fir.

expand to see more

Hebrew saphan (H5603) — to cover, to panel; Haggai 1:4, Jeremiah 22:14, and the king's house of cedar in 1 Kings 7:3.

Hebrew chaphah (H2645) — to overlay; the greater house cieled with fir and fine gold, 2 Chronicles 3:5.

Usage

"“Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses?” — the prophet audits the ceilings."

"“And this house lie waste” — the comparison that convicts."

"“That saith, I will build me a wide house… cieled with cedar” — luxury by unpaid wages is woe, not stewardship."
